headings.title: Introduction and Definition of Inhalation Therapy
headings.content: Inhalation therapy is a vital therapeutic modality in nursing care, involving the administration of pharmaceutical agents directly into the respiratory tract through the airways. By delivering medications in the form of gases, aerosols, or fine powders, this route targets the lungs directly, ensuring a rapid onset of pharmacological action while significantly minimizing systemic side effects. In the context of Nigerian healthcare settings, inhalation therapy is frequently utilized to manage acute and chronic respiratory conditions such as bronchial asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), and acute bronchospasm. The primary goal is to relieve airway obstruction, reduce inflammation, liquefy pulmonary secretions, and improve overall pulmonary ventilation and gas exchange. As nursing professionals, understanding the fundamentals of inhalation therapy is crucial for effective patient management, accurate administration, and optimal clinical outcomes. Nurses must be well-versed in the pharmacological agents used, the physiological mechanisms of drug deposition, and the various delivery systems available in clinical practice. Furthermore, effective administration requires careful patient assessment before, during, and after the procedure to evaluate the therapeutic response and promptly identify any adverse reactions. Mastery of this competency ensures patient safety and enhances adherence to long-term respiratory care regimens, which is particularly important in resource-constrained environments where prompt and efficient symptom control can prevent emergency hospital admissions.

headings.title: Anatomy and Physiology of the Respiratory Tract in Drug Delivery
headings.content: Understanding the anatomy and physiology of the respiratory tract is essential for nurses administering inhalation therapy, as the structural design of the airways directly influences how aerosolized drug particles are deposited. The respiratory system is divided into the upper respiratory tract (nasal cavity, pharynx, larynx) and the lower respiratory tract (trachea, bronchi, bronchioles, and alveoli). When a patient inhales a medicated aerosol, the particles travel through the mouth or nose and navigate the branching airways. Particle size is the single most critical factor determining where deposition occurs in the tract. Large particles, typically greater than 10 micrometers, tend to impact in the upper airways due to inertial impaction and are often filtered out by the nose and pharynx. Particles ranging from 2 to 5 micrometers are ideal for reaching the medium to small bronchioles, making them most effective for treating conditions like asthma. Meanwhile, very fine particles between 0.5 and 2 micrometers can penetrate deep into the alveolar region via sedimentation, though many may be exhaled if breath-holding techniques are not utilized. Physiological factors such as respiratory rate, tidal volume, and inspiratory flow velocity also dictate drug delivery; rapid, shallow breathing causes premature impaction in the upper airway, whereas slow, deep breaths followed by a breath-hold enhance deposition in the target lower airways.

headings.title: Types of Inhalation Equipment and Devices
headings.content: Various types of inhalation equipment and devices are utilized in clinical nursing practice to administer respiratory medications effectively. Selecting the appropriate device depends on the patient's age, cognitive ability, severity of illness, and manual dexterity. The three primary categories of devices are Metered-Dose Inhalers (MDIs), Dry Powder Inhalers (DPIs), and Nebulizers. MDIs deliver a specific amount of medication using a propellant gas; they are portable and efficient but require good hand-breath coordination. To overcome this coordination challenge, spacer devices or valved holding chambers are frequently attached to MDIs, reducing oral deposition and increasing lung penetration. DPIs are breath-actuated devices that deliver medication in a dry powder form without the need for propellants, requiring the patient to generate a sufficient inspiratory flow rate to fluidize and inhale the powder. Nebulizers, on the other hand, convert liquid medications into a fine mist using compressed air or ultrasonic waves. They are especially beneficial for infants, elderly patients, severely dyspneic individuals, or those unable to follow complex breathing instructions. Jet nebulizers and ultrasonic nebulizers are common variants found in hospital wards and emergency units across Nigeria. Nurses must understand the operational mechanics, advantages, and limitations of each device to ensure proper patient instruction and optimal therapeutic drug delivery.

headings.title: Indications and Clinical Uses in Nursing
headings.content: Inhalation therapy has broad indications and clinical uses in nursing care, primarily centered around managing respiratory distress and optimizing pulmonary function. Nurses frequently administer these treatments for patients experiencing acute bronchospasm, asthma exacerbations, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), cystic fibrosis, and pneumonia. The primary pharmacological agents delivered via this route include bronchodilators (such as short-acting beta-agonists like salbutamol and anticholinergics like ipratropium) which rapidly relax tightened airway smooth muscles. Additionally, anti-inflammatory agents, particularly inhaled corticosteroids, are prescribed for long-term control to reduce mucosal edema and hyper-reactivity in chronic conditions. Mucolytics and saline solutions are also indicated to hydrate thick, tenacious secretions, facilitating easier expectoration and clearing obstructed airways. Beyond emergency and maintenance therapy, nurses utilize inhalation techniques to administer prophylactic antibiotics in specific lung infections and to humidify dry medical gases. Recognizing the clinical indicators for inhalation therapy allows nurses to anticipate physician orders, initiate emergency interventions during acute respiratory compromise, and monitor the immediate effectiveness of bronchodilator therapy by assessing improvements in breath sounds, respiratory rate, and oxygen saturation levels.

headings.title: Preparation and Assessment of the Patient
headings.content: Thorough preparation and comprehensive patient assessment are critical prerequisites before initiating any inhalation therapy procedure. The nurse must first review the medical prescription to verify the correct drug, dosage, route, and timing according to the hospital's medication administration safety protocols. Assessment begins with evaluating the patient's baseline respiratory status, including respiratory rate, depth, effort, auscultation of breath sounds (noting wheezes, crackles, or diminished air entry), pulse oximetry readings, and vital signs. Furthermore, the nurse must assess the patient's level of consciousness, cognitive function, and manual dexterity to determine which delivery device (MDI, DPI, or nebulizer) is most appropriate for their unique needs. It is also essential to evaluate the patient's understanding of the procedure and their ability to follow instructions, such as performing a proper breath-hold or generating adequate inspiratory force. The nurse should inspect the oral cavity for signs of fungal infections or lesions, especially if the patient has been using steroid inhalers. Preparing the patient psychologically by explaining the steps of the procedure helps alleviate anxiety, fosters cooperation, and ensures the patient is positioned comfortably—ideally sitting upright or in a semi-Fowler's position to maximize lung expansion and optimize aerosol deposition.

headings.title: Step-by-Step Procedure for Administering Inhalation Therapy
headings.content: Executing a step-by-step procedure for administering inhalation therapy ensures maximum therapeutic benefit and patient safety. For a Metered-Dose Inhaler with a spacer, the nurse begins by washing hands and checking the rights of medication administration. The inhaler is shaken vigorously, and the cap is removed. The canister is inserted into the spacer device. The patient is instructed to exhale completely, emptying the lungs of normal air. The mouthpiece of the spacer is placed gently between the teeth, ensuring the lips are sealed tightly around it without biting or blocking the opening with the tongue. The nurse or patient then depresses the canister once to release a single puff of medication into the spacer chamber. The patient takes a slow, deep breath in through the mouth. If a whistle sound is heard, it indicates the inspiratory flow is too fast, and the patient must slow down. After inhaling, the patient removes the device and holds their breath for 5 to 10 seconds, or as long as comfortably possible, to allow particles to settle in the airways before exhaling slowly through pursed lips. If a second puff is prescribed, the nurse must wait about 30 to 60 seconds before repeating the process. For nebulizer therapy, the liquid medication is measured into the nebulizer cup, connected to an air source at 6 to 8 liters per minute, and the patient breathes normally through a mouthpiece or mask until the mist ceases. Post-procedure oral hygiene, such as rinsing the mouth with water, is mandatory, especially after corticosteroid use.

headings.title: Potential Complications and Safety Precautions
headings.content: While inhalation therapy is generally safe and effective, nurses must be vigilant regarding potential complications and implement strict safety precautions. Local side effects frequently include throat irritation, coughing, dry mouth, hoarseness of voice, and oral fungal infections (candidiasis) when using corticosteroids. Systemic adverse effects can also occur, particularly with high doses or frequent use of beta-agonists; these include tachycardia, palpitations, tremors, nervousness, and hypokalemia. Nurses must monitor vital signs closely during and after administration, especially in patients with pre-existing cardiovascular conditions. Safety precautions also extend to equipment hygiene. Nebulizers and spacers can easily become breeding grounds for bacterial and fungal pathogens if not cleaned, disinfected, and dried properly between uses, potentially leading to secondary respiratory infections. Oxygen safety is paramount when compressed air or oxygen tanks are used to drive nebulizers; nurses must enforce strict 'No Smoking' policies and keep equipment away from open flames. Furthermore, nurses should check medication expiration dates and ensure proper storage away from direct heat and moisture to maintain drug efficacy and prevent chemical degradation.

headings.title: Patient Education and Home Care Management
headings.content: Patient education and home care management are cornerstones of effective long-term respiratory nursing care. Empowering patients and their caregivers with comprehensive knowledge ensures adherence to prescribed regimens and prevents avoidable emergency room visits. Nurses must provide clear, demonstrated instructions on how to use their specific inhalation devices correctly, allowing the patient to perform a return demonstration to verify competence. Education should cover the difference between rescue medications (used for quick relief of acute symptoms) and controller medications (used daily to manage underlying inflammation), emphasizing that controller drugs must be taken consistently even when the patient feels well. Home care management also includes teaching patients how to monitor their peak expiratory flow rates using a peak flow meter, recognizing early warning signs of worsening respiratory status, and knowing when to seek emergency medical assistance. Furthermore, nurses must instruct patients on proper device maintenance, such as washing plastic spacer housings in mild soapy water and allowing them to air dry weekly. In Nigeria, where environmental dust and seasonal harmattan winds can severely trigger respiratory symptoms, nurses should counsel patients on environmental control measures, avoiding known allergens, and ensuring continuity of medication supply to promote holistic, independent self-management.
